syllabus.clause: Axum has no middleware system of its own; it is built entirely on tower::Service, so Tower middleware (timeouts, tracing, compression, authorization via tower-http) is shared with any Tower-based stack. Extractors, State, middleware::from_fn, and the 0.8 routing syntax (/{param}).

at.step: Axum's own documentation says so plainly: Axum doesn't have its own middleware system; it uses tower::Service, and that's what gets it timeouts, tracing, compression, and authorization for free
Measured: a real request to a path with a name in it came back with that exact name, pulled out by a real extractor, not a hand-written parser
Measured: three separate real requests came back with increasing values in a row, a real piece of shared state actually accumulating, not three fresh copies

Measured: a real middleware::from_fn layer genuinely modified a real response, and a real tower-http timeout genuinely cut off a handler that would have taken far longer, both running against real requests

items.item: axum doesn't have its own middleware system but instead uses tower::Service; this means axum gets timeouts, tracing, compression, authorization, and more, for free, and enables sharing middleware with applications written using hyper or tonic

items.item: a handler function is an async function that takes any number of extractors as arguments; an extractor is a type that implements FromRequest or FromRequestParts

items.item: from_fn creates a middleware from an async function; this function doesn't support extracting State directly, for that use from_fn_with_state

items.item: tower-http is a library that provides HTTP-specific middleware and utilities built on top of tower; all middleware uses the http and http-body crates, compatible with any library using those crates

items.item: The server under test binds to a real ephemeral TcpListener port (127.0.0.1:0) rather than a fixed port, so the same binary can run repeatedly in CI without a stale port-in-use conflict; the real local address is read back from the listener itself before the client connects to it.

at.step: Stand up a real, running Axum server with a route written in the newer /{param} syntax. Send a real request for a specific name through it. Does the handler actually receive that name, or does it need to parse the raw path itself?

items.item: The State measurement sends three sequential real HTTP requests rather than concurrent ones, specifically so the accumulated counter values (one, two, three in order) are deterministic; a concurrent version would still prove sharing, but the exact final count would depend on scheduling, which is not the claim under test here.

at.step: Measured: three separate real requests came back with increasing values in a row, a real piece of shared state actually accumulating, not three fresh copies

items.item: The from_fn middleware is verified by checking for a custom response header it injects, rather than by its side effects being merely assumed from the API working at all; the header's presence is the actual, falsifiable signal that the middleware genuinely ran against that specific real response.

at.step: Wrap that server in a real middleware::from_fn layer that touches every response, and separately, a real tower-http layer that cuts a handler off if it runs too long. Do both of those actually run against real requests, the same way any other Tower layer would?

items.item: The tower-http Timeout example uses TimeoutLayer::with_status_code rather than the deprecated TimeoutLayer::new, both to avoid a compiler warning and because the status-code variant makes the layer's own real effect (a request-timeout response, not a dropped connection) directly observable in the measured response's own status code.
